AWS Systems Manager Automation now automates operational tasks in Azure and Google Cloud

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (269 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS Systems Manager Automation now lets you create custom workflows (runbooks) that can automate operational tasks across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS resources.
  • It has been revealed that six new runbook actions call Azure and Google Cloud APIs, check a resource's state, and wait for operations to finish without custom code.
  • Sources indicate that this capability is available in all AWS Regions where you can create a Systems Manager Cloud Connector.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Systems Manager Automation now lets you create custom workflows (runbooks) that can automate operational tasks across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS resources. Automation helps you make changes safely at scale, such as remediating misconfigurations or cleaning up idle resources. Runbooks can roll out in controlled batches, pause for approval, and stop if errors pass a threshold. Instead of maintaining separate tools and credentials for each cloud, teams can now author and execute runbooks from a single place.

It has been revealed that six new runbook actions call Azure and Google Cloud APIs, check a resource's state, and wait for operations to finish without custom code. You can target Azure resources by subscription, region, resource group, resource type, and tag. Google Cloud resources can be targeted by project, zone, asset type, and label. For more complex logic, aws:executeScript now includes Azure and Google Cloud Python SDKs and gets short-lived credentials from your Systems Manager Cloud Connector, so you don't store secrets in runbooks. For example, you can stop tagged development virtual machines outside business hours or fix storage buckets that don't meet your security policy. To get started, use the AWS-provided runbooks that install the SSM Agent or the Amazon Inspector agent on your Azure or Google Cloud virtual machines, or create your own custom workflow.

Sources indicate that this capability is available in all AWS Regions where you can create a Systems Manager Cloud Connector. To learn more, see Run automations on multicloud resources in the AWS Systems Manager User Guide, or visit the AWS Systems Manager product page.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Sources indicate that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Industry observers note that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

It has been revealed that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

According to recent reports, we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Sources indicate that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

According to recent reports, training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but tech giant policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly upcoming solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

Recent findings suggest that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 reveals which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Recent findings suggest that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

According to recent reports, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

According to recent reports, the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

According to recent reports, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Industry observers note that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Industry observers note that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

According to recent reports, table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

Recent findings suggest that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Industry observers note that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Sources indicate that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

According to recent reports, for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each upgrade generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

Sources indicate that thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Industry observers note that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Sources indicate that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO patch.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

According to recent reports, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

Tech Report: What’s new in Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands.
  • In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation.
  • Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that as organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands. Moving from human scale to agent scale changes both how data pipelines run and how they are built: Teams and AI agents now use Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and agentic troubleshooting to build, submit, and diagnose Apache Spark pipelines while preparing multimodal datasets, performing feature engineering, and acting on live business signals around the clock. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud.

In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces:.

A newly introduced 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apache Spark 4.2, Java 25, Python 3.13 with Pixi, and Apache Iceberg 1.12, it is now available for both serverless and managed clusters.

A redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console and agentic troubleshooting: Onboard promptly with a newly introduced Overview page featuring a samples gallery, Lakehouse public datasets, and one-click VS Code authoring in Cloud Shell, manage all serverless and cluster workloads from a unified Jobs view, and use an AI agent to automatically diagnose job failures.

Third-party IDE integration with the Data Agent Kit: Configure MCP servers, skills, and API access to build and run Apache Spark pipelines directly from VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity.

Faster startups and Lightning Engine acceleration: Run on default Gen4 infrastructure with faster startups at no additional cost, and accelerate workloads with Lightning Engine for up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative.

This newly introduced runtime packages Apache Spark 4.2 (including Spark Declarative Pipelines and Real-Time Mode), Java 25, Scala 2.13, Apache Iceberg 1.12, Delta Lake 4.4, and Python 3.13 with Pixi for faster dependency management.

According to recent reports, managed Spark serverless and cluster workloads now run on the same modern stack whether written by a data engineer or generated by data engineering and data science skills in Gemini, Claude, and other large language models (LLMs). Teams can standardize on one set of component versions and move PySpark, Scala, and Spark SQL workloads between serverless and managed clusters.

Recent findings suggest that data teams should spend their time writing Spark logic rather than configuring infrastructure, hunting for the right job, or digging through driver and executor logs when something fails. Version 4.0 ships alongside a redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console built to take that operational work off their plate.

The refreshed console streamlines every stage of the Apache Spark lifecycle:.

Frictionless onboarding and one-click authoring: A redesigned Overview page helps developers get started immediately with an integrated samples gallery, pre-loaded Lakehouse public datasets, guided demos, and one-click authoring in VS Code through Cloud Shell.

Recent findings suggest that optimized defaults and reusable runtime profiles: Out-of-the-box performance defaults simplify job submission and cluster creation. With reusable runtime profiles (in preview) for batch and interactive workloads, platform admins can capture governed hardware, network, and autoscaling baselines once so developers can simply select a profile and run code.

Unified job, session, and fleet management: Engineers can submit and monitor batch jobs, interactive serverless sessions, and managed clusters from a single unified listing, backed by streamlined fleet management and redesigned detail views that surface key performance metrics and logs in one place.

Agentic troubleshooting: When a job fails or slows down, an AI agent analyzes logs, metrics, and query looks within existing IAM permissions to identify the likely root cause and recommend a fix, helping engineers promptly return a failed job to a healthy state.

Image 1: Gemini Cloud Assist investigates a failed Apache Spark job, forms a hypothesis, and points to the likely root cause without leaving the job page.

Image 2: One Jobs page for every Apache Spark workload across serverless and managed clusters, with tier and runtime version at a glance.

In a recent development, many data engineers and data scientists would rather never leave their editor. With the Data Agent Kit, they can build and run Apache Spark workloads from VS Code, Antigravity, Claude Code, and other agentic IDEs. Setup takes a few clicks: pick Apache Spark and the other services you use, and the kit configures Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agent skills, and API access for each one. From there, AI agents can generate, tune, and test Apache Spark pipelines on Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 without leaving the IDE.

Image 3: In VS Code, the Data Agent Kit sets up MCP servers, skills, and API access for Apache Spark and other services.

As practitioners and AI agents trigger short-running, ephemeral jobs on demand to prepare data, perform feature engineering, and answer ad-hoc queries, low startup latency and predictable price-performance are essential to avoiding a cost spiral. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, our performance-optimized serverless experience removes manual infrastructure tuning through three changes:.

Faster startups at no additional cost: On the serverless Premium tier, runtime and control-plane optimizations in version 4.0 deliver faster startup times than previous runtime versions across interactive sessions and short-running batch workloads at no additional cost.

Hardware acceleration by default: Fresh serverless 4.0 workloads run on the Premium tier by default, using Google Cloud's latest-generation Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk storage. Teams get our highest-efficiency compute and storage fleet without picking machine types or configuring disks, while aligning infrastructure tiering directly with workload urgency.

In a recent development, software acceleration with Lightning Engine: Our native C++ vectorized execution engine, Lightning Engine, is available in the 4.0 runtime and delivers up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative, along with up to 4.9x faster performance compared to running open-source Apache Spark with zero code changes. Built on Apache Gluten and Velox with Google-specific optimizations, Lightning Engine compiles Apache Spark DataFrame, Dataset, and Spark SQL query plans into native SIMD instructions. For lakehouse storage, built-in intelligent caching accelerates file scan times on Apache Iceberg tables by up to 50%. Separately, for workloads querying BigQuery, Lightning Engine's native reader uses Apache Arrow streams to accelerate BigQuery reads by up to 40% compared to default BigQuery reads in Managed Service for Apache Spark. In the 4.0 runtime, Lightning Engine expands support to ARM processors, Ubuntu images, and native vectorized readers for Apache ORC and CSV alongside Apache Parquet, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake.

Industry observers note that "We were facing not only processing challenges, we were facing management overhead across thousands of servers in our ecosystem, so we migrated to serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark. We moved from managing infrastructure to a no-ops infrastructure. Not only did it help us overcome maintenance and cluster management challenges, it helped us optimize our costs at scale to meet our business SLAs. Apache Spark is no longer just compute for us; it is a strategic business accelerator."—Saurabh Kumar, Senior Director of Data Engineering, Lowe's.

When autonomous agents and production pipelines run around the clock, tying a workload to a single machine shape or zone can stall downstream decisions when regional demand spikes. Without dedicated reservations, cloud service providers may not always have available capacity during peak demand. We are introducing infrastructure fungibility for serverless deployments to improve resource availability for all customers:.

Industry observers note that serverless infrastructure fungibility and fallback: Serverless 4.0 workloads are no longer tied to one VM instance family, disk type, or zone. The platform selects from several latest-generation VM instance families and disk types across zones in the region. If the preferred infrastructure is constrained during a local demand peak, the service automatically chooses the best available infrastructure in the same region instead of failing the job. Once capacity returns, workloads go back to the default Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk infrastructure.

Data Compute Unit (DCU) quotas: Quotas for serverless deployments are now set in DCUs rather than per machine family. Because the platform selects the VM instance family, admins manage one unified DCU quota instead of separate CPU quotas for each machine type.

It has been revealed that A borderless lakehouse breaks down walled gardens by connecting operational, analytical, and cross-cloud data in open formats without moving it. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, Apache Iceberg ships directly in the runtime image, and every workload automatically has access to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. Teams no longer have to configure a lakehouse metastore with Apache Spark or complete prerequisites such as setting up Google Cloud Storage (GCS) directories beforehand, so they can focus straight on writing business logic. Version 4.0 also eliminates the need for GCS staging buckets and uses end-user credentials by default.

Through the Lakehouse runtime catalog, Managed Service for Apache Spark, BigQuery, and AlloyDB can directly read and write the same Apache Iceberg tables on GCS without ETL pipelines or data copies. Everything registered in the Lakehouse runtime catalog automatically surfaces in Knowledge Catalog, which enriches metadata and business context so AI agents and Gemini can query and reason over tables curated with Apache Spark with high accuracy, governed access controls, and lower token costs.

Recent findings suggest that to see how these capabilities come together across end-to-end architectures, read our Google Cloud Apache Spark in the Agentic Era whitepaper. The whitepaper walks through practical design patterns for multimodal data preparation, large-scale feature engineering, and connecting AI agents to governed Apache Iceberg tables through MCP tools and Knowledge Catalog.

Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 is available for serverless and managed cluster deployments across all Managed Service for Apache Spark regions. The fastest way to try version 4.0 is the Data Agent Kit: install it in VS Code, Claude Code, or Antigravity to build and run Apache Spark workloads on version 4.0 with AI agents right from your IDE. You can also start from the newly introduced Overview page in the Google Cloud console, which walks you from code to a running job.

To learn more, read the Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 documentation for serverless deployments and managed clusters, and try the hands-on Lightning Engine codelab.

as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform.

Industry observers note that the Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled.

According to recent reports, iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis.

None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply.

In a recent development, “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” indicates Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”.

Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.

It has been revealed that “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”.

It has been revealed that what was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime.

Recent findings suggest that the team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that rolls out a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.

Sources indicate that “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Customers can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.

The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.

Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.

“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”.

According to recent reports, the sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.

The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one.

It has been revealed that “We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.”.

That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration.

Delegating execution at scale creates a newly introduced challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do.

iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.

The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.

The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” indicates Coelho.

This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API.

The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement.

Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it.

“While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.”.

It has been revealed that routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment.

The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers.

In a recent development, “The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.”.

The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.

The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks, consuming more than 27 billion tokens, at an average cost of US$0.04 per run.

After migrating to the Remote Agents Platform, the internal security platform more than doubled both the accuracy of its fixes and the number of vulnerabilities resolved.

Coverage extends across iFood’s more than 15,000 code repositories.

All runs use GPT‑5.6 Luna, chosen for its balance of intelligence, efficiency, and speed.

Structured Outputs ensures that each session returns a result that follows a predefined contract, whether positive or negative.

Product teams have moved from building fragmented solutions to delegating agentic execution through a REST API.

The bottleneck is often the runtime, not the use case. Several teams already knew what they wanted to automate; they lacked an environment in which to run it.

Industry observers note that combine deterministic steps with agentic execution. Cloning, publishing, and making artifacts available don’t require a model; the complex task in between does.

Treat cost per run as an architectural decision. At scale, the cost per task determines what is feasible to automate.

Sources indicate that require outputs to follow a contract. Without a structured response, there’s no way to know at scale whether the agent achieved its objective.

Sources indicate that asynchronous execution is the real productivity gain. The value lies in not having to monitor the work, rather than completing it faster while watching over it.

Expose agentic capabilities through an internal API so other teams can use them without rebuilding the infrastructure.

Isolate each run in its own sandbox, with your ecosystem’s toolchains already installed.

Choose a model by considering intelligence, cost, and speed together, rather than a single benchmark.

Use structured outputs to classify success and failure automatically.

Start with an internal user with a clear pain point and high volume—at iFood, that was the security platform.

The team looks to bring the platform to many more use cases across iFood, expanding the range of internal products that delegate agentic execution to it—with cost per task determining whether that expansion can be sustained.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • Sources indicate that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

Sources indicate that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

It has been revealed that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We strategy to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Sources indicate that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

In a recent development, each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel strategy use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Recent findings suggest that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS plans, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal.

Developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators.

One of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. To modernize the platform’s architecture, TCS partnered with the customer to achieve a landmark milestone: migrating DynaPORT to a modern, cloud-based architecture.

Industry observers note that the Port Operator & TCS partnered with Google Cloud to execute an ambitious cloud modernization journey. Modeled after the architectural principles of high-velocity Google Cloud enterprise transformations—this case study details the systematic deconstruction of legacy technical debt, the strategic rationale and enterprise differentiators of choosing AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, the target Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and AlloyDB cloud-native architecture, the heterogeneous migration of over 1.2 million lines of code using Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS).

Industry observers note that enterprise logistics platforms that evolve over decades inevitably accumulate architectural debt, particularly through tightly coupled components. DynaPORT Cargo followed this pattern: successive releases and architectural transitions gradually transformed the platform into a classic multi-tier monolith, with its components carrying significant technical debt.

Over years of optimization for sub-millisecond on-premises database round-trips, fundamental business logic had been progressively migrated out of the application tier and embedded directly into the database engine. In the DynaPORT Cargo module alone, the core schema contained:.

262 Packages containing over 1.2 million lines of code.

54 Stored Procedures, 53 Functions, and 63 Database Triggers.

Cross-schema User-Defined Types (UDTs).

Sources indicate that critical business operations—such as multi-tiered marine invoice tariff calculations, dynamic slab rating, berth allocation planning, yard truck assignments, and autonomous error logging—were entirely governed by complex, multi-thousand-line PL/SQL procedures. The database was no longer merely a relational persistence store; it was the primary execution engine of the enterprise.

Industry observers note that the application tier was hosted on monolithic WebLogic and WildFly application servers running on static on-premises virtual machines. The application relied on legacy Java Enterprise features, including Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs), custom Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) dialects, and heavy configuration state. Modules including Revenue Management, Berth Planning, Gate Operations, and Reporting shared common JVM heaps across application servers. A performance spike in batch invoice generation could starve memory from real-time Handheld Terminals (HHT) used by container crane operators on the quayside.

Because business logic was fragmented across Java application binaries and raw database packages, continuous delivery was practically non-existent:.

Manual Deployment Runbooks: Releases required multi-hour maintenance windows involving manual execution of sequential SQL scripts, package recompilations, and server restarts.

High Regression Risk: In the legacy schema with 262 interdependent packages, modifying a single package specification frequently invalidated dozens of dependent functions, views, and synonyms, triggering cascading runtime failures.

Environment Drift: Development, testing, and production environments suffered from configuration divergence, requiring lengthy manual reconciliation before any production cutover.

Licensing fees scaled linearly with physical CPU core counts, penalizing the business whenever hardware was scaled to accommodate peak cargo vessel traffic. Furthermore, high-availability setups required complex shared storage arrays, specialized interconnects, and heavy administrative overhead from dedicated database administrators (DBAs).

When architecting the cloud transformation, the joint architecture teams from the customer, TCS, and Google Cloud evaluated two fundamentally different modernization strategies:.

Strategy A: Database-Agnostic Migration.

Strategy B: Modernization using AlloyDB.

Extract all business logic from the database tier and rewrite it into Java application-tier services (HQL / Spring Data).

Retain optimized procedural logic in the database tier, converting to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL on AlloyDB.

It has been revealed that massive. Complete rewrite of thousands of data access objects, ORM mappings, and transaction boundaries.

Moderate. Focused remediation of syntax, metadata, and database dialect differences; application remains stable.

Multiple person-years; prohibitive time-to-market.

Target delivery achievable in agile sprints; low operational disruption.

Network latency amplification due to multiple network hops for complex set operations previously run in-database.

Native in-engine execution with sub-millisecond response times, backed by AlloyDB’s accelerated storage and compute engine.

Rejected due to timeline risks and massive business disruption.

Selected as the winning enterprise target path.

The target cloud architecture was designed according to the Google Cloud Architecture Framework, transforming the monolithic JEE middleware into modern containerized microservices orchestrated on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), coupled with an enterprise AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster.

Industry observers note that the cornerstone of the migration was converting over 1.2 million lines of deeply intertwined Oracle PL/SQL procedural logic into PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. The team utilized Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS) with its built-in Conversion Workspaces and Gemini-assisted AI code refactoring to accelerate bulk transformations.

Industry observers note that while DMS automatically converted the majority of standard DDL constructs, functions, and queries, the remaining (~15%) involved complex Oracle proprietary idioms that required targeted engineering remediation. Couple of examples of the manual intervention.

Technical Pattern & Remediation.

Modernized AlloyDB PL/pgSQL Equivalent.

Architectural Remediation & Runtime Impact.

TYPE_L := array_append(TYPE_L, rec); or TYPE_L[cardinality(TYPE_L)+1] := rec;.

Replaced unsupported .EXTEND method on nested tables with native PostgreSQL array concatenation and dynamic index expansion.

SELECT ROWNUM FROM PTY_IM WHERE ROWNUM <= N;.

SELECT s.idx FROM generate_series(1, N) AS s(idx);.

Eliminated physical dummy table hacks (PTY_IM) in favor of in-memory, set-returning generator functions with zero disk I/O.

Sources indicate that in April 2026, the modernized DynaPORT platform on Google Cloud went live in production at one of the newest ports in India, achieving a seamless, low downtime cutover. By Aug’26, 3 more terminals have gone live on this.

Modernized Google Cloud & AlloyDB Stack.

Variable query latency during batch spikes; table bloat requiring manual DBA reindexing.

Upto 2x transactional throughput, sub-second read query responses, automated ML vacuuming and memory optimization.

Complex SAN failover; multi-minute outages during planned database maintenance.

Sub-second automatic failover, 99.99% availability SLA inclusive of maintenance, zero transaction loss.

Multi-week release cycles; high-risk manual database patching; frequent regression concerns.

Containerized rolling updates on GKE and non-blocking transactional DDL deployments in AlloyDB.

Punitive per-core enterprise licenses; high on-prem hardware and maintenance overhead.

About 50% reduction in database TCO; completely open-source compatible with transparent, predictable cloud pricing.

Rigid vertical hardware limits; slow hardware procurement cycles.

Instantaneous horizontal elasticity across GKE container pods and AlloyDB read pools.

The successful cloud migration of DynaPORT yields three fundamental architectural lessons for enterprise IT leaders:.

Sources indicate that do Not Throw Away Proven Intellectual Property: Fully rewriting mission-critical procedural logic into application code is often a high-risk anti-pattern. Migrating from Oracle PL/SQL to open PL/pgSQL on an accelerated engine like AlloyDB preserves decades of tested business rules while modernizing the infrastructure platform.

Select Database Engines Built for Cloud Realities: Standard open-source relational engines often struggle with extreme enterprise throughput without extensive tuning. AlloyDB’s disaggregated storage architecture, columnar acceleration, and built-in ML intelligence provide the enterprise muscle needed to replace legacy commercial database engines.

Containerize Application Workloads on GKE: Decoupling the application tier into independently scalable container pods on Google Kubernetes Engine provides the elasticity and resilience necessary to absorb rapid operational surges without affecting core database stability.

In a recent development, schedule a Google Cloud Architecture Blueprint Workshop with your Google Cloud Account Field team today. We will engage as an important stakeholder to evaluate your current legacy setup and help design a low-risk, high-performance migration pathway using Google Cloud services like AlloyDB and Google Kubernetes Engine.

To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her dot⁠ changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask.

For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination. Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work.

Sources indicate that she brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages.

Sources indicate that next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through ChatGPT⁠(opens in a new window) plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s prepares for the following year.

In a recent development, using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina.

When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina claims.

According to recent reports, aria can also spot things Marina hadn’t thought to check. When Marina asked Aria to reuse pricing from an earlier proposal, it noticed that the original renewal date didn’t match the timing she remembered. Aria flagged the discrepancy and left the date out of the newly introduced draft.

Recent findings suggest that marina uses the Gmail and Slack plugins in ChatGPT to catch up on conversations, find open tasks, and see where the team needs her. Aria checks for messages that need Marina’s attention. While Marina was offline, Aria spotted a reply she had been waiting for and let her know it included an invitation for a call that morning.

In a recent development, marina also uses Aria to talk through ideas, find conversations, check an account’s history in the CRM, or open and assign tasks in Asana. She often briefs Aria by phone while she travels.

Recent findings suggest that marina loves that her dot works in the tools she already uses. When Aria writes a draft, Marina can leave comments in Google Docs exactly where she wants changes. On longer documents, she asks Aria to use suggesting mode so she can see what changed.

According to recent reports, aria also keeps up with changes in shared work without being asked. For a conference presentation, Marina created the deck and a colleague added two slides. “Aria noticed the new slides, updated the speaker notes without being asked, and let me know,” Marina states.

Sources indicate that marina chooses which information Aria can access and always reviews outgoing email. She can keep work moving without handing over the final call.

In a recent development, when Marina prepared an AI 101 session on agents, she used Aria to help build the lesson. 📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1650 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges.
  • According to recent reports, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

Other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

According to recent reports, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

At Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous organization ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

According to recent reports, why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

According to recent reports, once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

Qualitative: "A new analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

Recent findings suggest that A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Industry observers note that both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated tech giant’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

Industry observers note that figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

First, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the organization's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

Industry observers note that in the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

Given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

Computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

Sources indicate that A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

It has been revealed that our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human users. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

Industry observers note that we also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

Generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

Synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their users — will thank you.

Block Scholes, a provider of institutional digital asset derivatives data and analytics, has extended its offering to supply continuous, round-the-clock market data covering pre-IPO firms, equities, indices, commodities and digital assets.

Industry observers note that because the feeds never pause, on-chain trading venues are now able to price, margin and settle options even while traditional markets are shut. This means positions can be valued at any point in the day or week, rather than depending on the price set when markets close on a Friday.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer indicates its data underpins more than 90% of on-chain options volume, which has positioned it as a benchmark source of real-world asset (RWA) option data. Its client base spans traditional financial services groups as well as digital asset-native businesses.

Sources indicate that all of the major on-chain options platforms offering RWA options rely on Block Scholes data, including Derive, Hypercall and Paradex, it claimed. The firm also operates its own oracle, allowing venues to draw index prices, volatility surfaces and option marks from a single independent provider instead of combining multiple separate feeds.

It has been revealed that block Scholes offers continuous pricing now spans every asset class it covers, with seventeen underlying RWAs available at present. These include equities such as Apple, Nvidia and SpaceX, commodities such as oil, and pre-IPO names including Anthropic and OpenAI.

Industry observers note that block Scholes CEO and founder Eamonn Gashier remarked, “With 24/7 trading becoming an increasing reality, Block Scholes is at the forefront of providing market participants with the ability to trade around the clock. This allows them to manage exposure and risk during weekends and public holidays, meaning investors and traders can react to market movements at any time of day.

“With clients ranging from data providers and traditional finance firms to digital asset exchanges and asset managers, we are seeing a rapid growing demand for our pricing and data feeds, making us the industry standard setters.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inverite, a Canadian risk infrastructure business that converts permissioned financial data into reliable intelligence, has rolled out Portfolio IQ, a tool built to help lenders relate past and current loan performance to the financial data and risk insights gathered when a loan was first issued.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced solution pushes the firm’s risk intelligence offering past the point of the initial credit decision. It achieves this by matching the information held on a borrower at origination with the way the loan actually performed over its full term.

At the heart of the launch is Inverite’s upcoming Loan Performance API. Through it, lenders can submit structured information on historical and ongoing repayment results, which can then be traced back to the original financial data, the borrower’s Default IQ score and the lending decision itself. The result is an ongoing feedback loop that equips both lenders and Inverite’s own risk team with the information required to assess how a portfolio performs as time goes on.

Lenders can apply Portfolio IQ to a range of tasks, including validating models after the fact, analysing score bands and cut-off points, monitoring portfolios, reviewing strategy and building tailored risk models.

According to recent reports, inverite CEO Karim Nanji mentioned, “Every lending decision is an opportunity to learn from the outcome. Portfolio IQ connects our predictive financial intelligence with actual loan performance, giving lenders a clearer understanding of how their risk strategies perform over time. It also expands the value of Inverite’s intelligence infrastructure by supporting our customers beyond the initial lending decision.”.
