  • According to recent reports, there were a total of 15 FinTech deals this week, with a combined capital pool of $614m.
  • Sources indicate that one of the most notable aspects of this week’s deals is the global reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a diverse week for FinTech deals this week, with 12 different countries home to at least one deal.

According to recent reports, there were a total of 15 FinTech deals this week, with a combined capital pool of $614m. This represented a slight downturn on the previous week, which saw $991m raised across 17 deals.

Sources indicate that one of the most notable aspects of this week’s deals is the global reach. Typically, the US dominates the space and often accounts for more than half of deals. While the US still took the top spot for deals, there were just three. The only other place to record multiple deals was the UK, with two.

In a recent development, the lion share of funding this week was attributed to just two deals, both of which secured over $200m. US-based Sanctuary Wealth’s $250m growth capital round was the biggest deal of the week. It plans to use the capital to expand its specialist expertise, win new business and complete acquisitions. Germany-based Pliant was a close second, securing €200m ($218.7m).

In a recent development, sweden-based Trustly, which offers account-to-account payments built on Open Banking infrastructure, was the third biggest deal of the week, closing on $60m. The remaining FinTech deals this week were all $20m and under.

In terms of location, the other two US companies were Supertake and Metano, while the UK-based FinTechs were Acorda and Napo.

Europe had a strong week for deals. In addition to the UK, Germany and Sweden, there were also deals in Norway (Audun) and Spain (Reversa).

It has been revealed that there were two deals in the middle east, with the UAE’s Sooner and Jordan’s invoiceQ. South America also had two FinTech deals, with Brazil’s IKKB and Argentina’s Lemon both closing deals. Finishing off the deals of the week were two deals in south Asia with India-based Ionic Wealth and Pakistan-based Neem.

It has been revealed that with the US’ weekly dominance in deal activity it is easy to assume it would also dominate in deal size. However, research from FinTech Global this week found that seven different countries were represented among the top 10 FinTech deals in Q1 – Q3 2026.

As for subsectors, WealthTech reigned supreme with four deals in total. The WealthTech companies were Sanctuary Wealth, Supertake, Ionic Wealth and Lemon. It was followed close behind by the infrastructure and enterprise software space, which recorded three deals. These were invoiceQ, IKKBand Neem.

According to recent reports, as for the other subsectors, there were two deals apiece in PayTech (Pliant and Trustly), RegTech (Acorda and Reversa) and marketplace lending (Sooner and Audun). Finishing off, there was one deal each in CyberTech (Metano) and InsurTech (Napo).

Here are the 15 FinTech deals covered on FinTech Global this week:.

Sanctuary Wealth has received a $250m growth capital commitment from its existing backer Kennedy Lewis Investment Management.

The deal hands Sanctuary a larger pool of money to finance the ambitions, equity sales and succession plans of the firms on its platform.

The fresh funding will be used to widen the specialist expertise available to Sanctuary’s Partner Firms, helping them serve clients across a broader range of needs, win fresh business and complete acquisitions.

Sanctuary will also gain more room to supply capital directly to Partner Firm owners, whether they want to fund expansion, cash out part of their stake or get ready for a leadership handover.

Kennedy Lewis, a multi-strategy private credit manager overseeing roughly $40bn in assets, has structured its commitment as $50m in mandatory convertible debt alongside a $200m delayed-draw term loan.

In addition, the investor has chosen to turn its current outstanding convertible debt holding in Sanctuary into equity. The relationship between the two firms dates back to 2022, and since that first investment Sanctuary has doubled its count of Partner Firms and nearly tripled the assets on its platform.

Over eight years, Sanctuary has built a platform designed to help advisors leaving wirehouses establish their own independent businesses. Its scale and depth have drawn growing attention from advisors and independent wealth managers, prompting the firm to introduce additional affiliation models that give sophisticated advisors greater choice in how they pursue their goals.

Pliant, the Berlin-based B2B payments FinTech, has lined up more than €200m in fresh debt financing capacity across three separate deals with Ascory Bank AG and Viola Credit.

The newly introduced capacity is aimed at backing rising credit card transaction volumes and the credit lines Pliant extends to customers throughout Europe.

Commercial card issuing has particular liquidity demands, chiefly the need to fund customer credit balances and to post collateral for card scheme settlement. The newly introduced structures provide secured financing against both of these needs, allowing Pliant to handle larger volumes of transactions without compromising the efficiency of its funding model.

Two of the three deals come from Ascory Bank, which has partnered with Pliant for several years. One is a securitisation backed by receivables from Pliant’s European corporate credit card operations. The other covers the collateral needed for Visa’s settlement process, known as the Visa Prefunding Solution, giving Pliant the liquidity to keep pace with growing card activity.

Sources indicate that the third deal expands Pliant’s current growth debt facility with Viola Credit and includes an option to raise the amount available. Taken together, the agreements are expected to underpin Pliant’s planned European growth for a minimum of two years.

The debt package comes shortly after Pliant revealed an $80m Series C round, which is earmarked for international expansion and further work on its AI-powered payment infrastructure. The upcoming facilities sit alongside that equity investment, adding capacity specifically for the European commercial card business.

Founded in 2020, Pliant runs a modular B2B payments platform that brings together commercial card issuing, payment accounts, FX and spend management for both businesses and AI agents. Its customers span travel, e-commerce, insurance and AI-native technology, while FinTechs, software platforms and banks build their own commercial payment products on its infrastructure. Through its API-first platform, AI agents and applications can tap into regulated payment rails with permissions, controls and auditability included.

Trustly, the Stockholm-headquartered Pay by Bank specialist, has secured $60m in new capital as it moves to reposition payment data as a source of commercial intelligence for the merchants it serves.

In a recent development, according to FinSMEs, Nordic Capital, Alfvén & Didrikson and BlackRock all participated in the round. The Swedish firm aims to channel the money into building new AI-powered products designed to extract insight from transaction flows.

Its stated aim is to give businesses sharper tools for attracting customers, keeping them engaged over a longer period and anticipating risk before it materialises.

The raise marks a notable strategic direction for the tech giant. Rather than treating a payment as the end point of a transaction, Trustly intends to use the data generated at checkout as a lever for growth and protection, a shift that could change how merchants evaluate their payment providers.

In a recent development, trustly offers account-to-account payments built on Open Banking infrastructure, allowing consumers to pay directly from their bank accounts with speed and security, in real time. Its network links more than 9,000 merchants with in excess of 650 million consumers, drawing on connections to 12,000 banks across upwards of 30 markets. Well-known names including PayPal, Virgin Media O2 and Booking.com count among its partners.

Supertake, a platform that uses AI agents to convert people’s market beliefs into stock portfolios, has secured $20m in seed funding to scale its business.

Venture firm Adjacent, through Nico Wittenborn, led the investment, with Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV) also taking part, according to a report from TechCrunch.

A number of angel investors joined the round, among them Nat Friedman, right now head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch, product manager Nikita Bier, investor Scott Belsky and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase executive now serving as a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

The latest capital comes after a $2m pre-seed round.

Supertake intends to use the money to grow its headcount across functions such as engineering, design and growth marketing.

Supertake’s stated mission is to make investing a meritocracy. People describe a conviction in everyday language, such as “Everyone will be on peptides”, and the platform builds an investment strategy around it, which is then run by frontier AI agents. Any user anywhere can follow and share these strategies, meaning ideas are judged on their performance rather than on whether their creator has time to monitor markets constantly.

Sooner, a UAE home-buying platform that funds half of a buyer’s down payment, has secured $20m in seed funding as it sets out to change how residents of the country purchase property.

The round drew backing from Nuwa Capital, Amwal Capital Partners, 500 Global, Annex Investments, Alserkal Group, Axeed LLC, Plus VC (+VC), 21 Ventures and Iliad Partners, along with a group of angel investors.

According to recent reports, the startup is tackling a long-standing hurdle in the UAE property market, where purchasing a home has traditionally required buyers to find 20% of the price in cash upfront. Under Sooner’s model, buyers contribute 10% at the outset while the tech giant covers the remaining half of the deposit using its own capital. That portion is then paid back in monthly instalments alongside the buyer’s mortgage over a term of between 12 and 60 months.

Industry observers note that with the fresh capital in place, Sooner is aiming to facilitate more than AED 1bn worth of home purchases during 2027. The firm describes this target as an initial step towards helping a generation of tenants move into ownership.

It has been revealed that sooner focuses on salaried buyers living in the UAE who want to purchase a ready-built property in Dubai. The process begins with a roughly two-minute check that indicates consumers which homes fall within their budget, without affecting their credit score. The tech giant then arranges a first-time buyer mortgage pre-approval with a suitable bank, supported by a lowest mortgage rate guarantee, and approves the down payment support. Buyers can then book viewings through the platform and complete the purchase of their chosen property.

Ionic Wealth, a technology-driven wealth management platform owned by Angel One, has secured Rs177 crore ($19m) in a strategic funding round to power its next stage of expansion.

The round was backed by Angel One alongside a group of marquee families, and brings the total amount raised by the tech giant to around Rs466 crore ($50m).

All investors from the earlier round returned for this one. The investor base includes prominent business families, Bollywood personalities, FinTech entrepreneurs, global CXOs, board advisors and media houses.

It has been revealed that the investment follows a period of rapid growth. Within two years, Ionic Wealth has pushed its assets under management (AUM) beyond Rs16,000 crore. It now serves more than 2,900 high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients across over 12 cities, with a team of more than 100 private bankers.

Ionic Wealth intends to use the fresh capital to strengthen its portfolio-led proposition and global capabilities, bring AI into its WealthTech experience, grow its UHNI business and widen its presence both in India and overseas.

In a recent development, the firm described the funds as patient capital, which will let it build on its early bets. These include using technology to scale its HNI offering, advancing global investing through GIFT City, opening up fractional access through the Accredited Investor framework and SIFs, and creating a distinct UHNI offering for India’s leading families.

It has been revealed that operating under the Ionic Wealth brand, Angel One Wealth Limited is a wholly owned subsidiary of Angel One Limited, one of India’s major FinTech platforms with a user base of over 40 million. Ionic Wealth is an omnichannel WealthTech platform that aims to rethink wealth management for India’s emerging HNIs and UHNIs.

Sources indicate that it gives clients access to exclusive investment opportunities across asset classes, a round-the-clock digital experience through its app, and domain specialists who build strategic prepares suited to each client’s wealth journey. The firm uses technology to generate sharper insights, boost team productivity and support scale.

Metano has come out of stealth with $12m in seed capital as enterprises struggle to keep autonomous software under control across their technology estates.

Sierra Ventures headed the round, which also drew backing from Correlation Ventures, High Alpha and 360 ONE.

The business is led by co-founders Neelima Rustagi, who serves as CEO, and Ratnesh Pandey, its CTO, with the leadership team bringing security backgrounds from ServiceNow, Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, FireEye and Microsoft.

The launch lands at a moment when companies are rolling out AI agents on employee devices, in coding tools, across cloud systems and inside SaaS applications. Each new deployment widens a scattered attack surface.

Current security products tend to guard a single layer of infrastructure, leaving teams without the end-to-end view and behavioural insight required to protect agents that move between those layers on their own.

According to recent reports, AI agents also differ from traditional software because they act and decide on the fly, frequently with valid credentials and sanctioned tools. Their conduct can shift depending on the prompts they receive, the outside material they consume and the conditions they run in, so dangers may stay hidden during early testing and only surface later.

Metano tackles this by merging three functions into a single control layer. First, it locates both sanctioned and shadow AI agents, along with MCP servers, skills and software packages, and maps the permissions and exposure attached to each.

Second, it interprets agent conduct through Hive, a live context graph that links tasks, identities, tools, data access and actions over the course of a session, allowing analysts to spot anomalies and judge whether an agent is acting in line with its purpose.

Third, it applies guardrails directly where agents run, including activity that never passes through conventional network gateways, so centrally set policies can halt harmful actions in the moment. The platform is designed to scale alongside a organization’s maturity in deploying agents.

invoiceQ has secured $5m in a Series A round that surpassed its original fundraising goal, giving it fresh capital as governments across its markets push businesses towards mandatory digital invoicing.

Manara Ventures and Next Ventures co-led the investment. They were joined by Orange Ventures, the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund (ISSF) and the Jordan Small and Medium Enterprises Fund (SME Fund Jo), with the latter now backing the firm for a second time.

The business already counts over 1,400 corporate customers and has built up a substantial set of regulatory credentials. It holds qualification from Saudi Arabia’s Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) and meets the requirements of Jordan’s Income and Sales Tax Department (ISTD). The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) and the Oman Tax Authority (OTA) have both recognised it as an Approved Service Provider (ASP), and it also operates as a certified Peppol Access Point (AP) and Service Metadata Publisher (SMP).

In a recent development, mohannad Tobal, Mohammad Bassit, Fadi Al Jabali and Amer Ayyad established invoiceQ, which offers a cloud-based SaaS platform that allows companies to automatically generate, handle, send and store invoices that satisfy tax rules, all from a single system. Its technology connects with existing ERP, POS, accounting, e-commerce, banking and payment software, meaning clients can meet regulatory obligations without overhauling the tools they already rely on.

Audun, an AI-native debt collection start-up, has secured $3m in pre-seed funding as it sets out to overhaul one of the most manual corners of financial services.

The round drew support from Alliance VC, Y Combinator, Robinhood Ventures, Skyfall Ventures and FirstDegree, along with a group of angel investors.

It has been revealed that audun is taking a different route from most innovators in the space. For years, change in debt collection has largely meant building software and selling it to collection agencies. Rather than offering another product of that kind, Audun has set itself up as a licensed agency in its own right. It is already recovering money for clients using its own platform, which handles every stage of a case, from the opening reminder through to the final payment.

The company argues that technology is moving faster than ever, yet collection practices look much as they did two decades ago. In its view, every debtor is pushed through an identical routine, while case handlers are tied up with repetitive admin. Audun believes the distance between what technology makes possible and what the sector actually provides is now wider than at any point before.

Audun’s platform takes over the routine, administrative side of collection so that its staff can devote their attention to the conversations where human judgement matters most.

IKKB, a financial management platform for companies operating across borders, has closed a $3m seed round to secure regulatory licences and develop fresh products for its multi-currency business account.

It has been revealed that the investment was led by Canary. According to the announcement, the capital will help IKKB obtain the licences it needs to operate as a regulated institution in each of its markets. It will also fund further products built on top of the core account. The firm already has licensing applications under way in Brazil, the US and Canada.

According to recent reports, canary mentioned it first met co-founders Edward Konig and Rafael Katalan in August 2025 and tracked their progress for over a year before investing. The investor said the pair learned rapidly, made difficult decisions with long-term goals in mind and achieved a great deal on limited funding. Canary believes a growing number of companies now operate internationally from launch, while the financial infrastructure supporting them remains slow, costly and fragmented.

IKKB’s offering has grown considerably in a short time. Just over a year ago, its product had a single function, converting PIX payments into US dollars. It has since become a multi-currency account for businesses, holding balances in BRL, USD, EUR and MXN. The account connects to local payment rails in Brazil, the US, Europe and Mexico, and offers corporate cards in BRL and USD. The team developed the platform internally on modest capital and prioritised regulatory work from the outset.

Recent findings suggest that the company is focused on giving Latin American businesses a global account. Firms can manage international payments, foreign exchange and treasury from a single platform. The service operates on stablecoin rails and applies AI to provide additional services alongside the account. IKKB offers accounts, cards, currency exchange, payments and treasury management.

Acorda, a London-based anti-fraud startup set up by three former Monzo employees, has secured £1.8m in a pre-seed round as it builds a network that lets banks and payment providers pool scam intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that according to DealRoom, Eileen Burbidge has backed the round. The startup will put the capital towards bringing banks and payment firms onto its data-sharing network.

The platform gives financial institutions a secure way to exchange scam risk indicators linked to the person or business receiving a payment, in the moments before the funds leave the sender’s account.

Recent findings suggest that with this information, the sending bank can judge how risky the recipient is before releasing the transfer. Acorda’s aim is to reduce the number of scams that succeed while also lowering the volume of legitimate payments wrongly flagged as fraudulent.

Acorda operates a fraud data-sharing network designed for banks and payment providers, focused on preventing scams at the point of payment rather than identifying losses once money has already moved.

Reversa, a Madrid-based RegTech firm developing artificial intelligence agents to handle regulatory tasks for businesses and public bodies, has secured €750,000 in fresh capital, which includes a pre-seed round headed by Itnig.

Sources indicate that itnig, the investment vehicle of the founders of Factorial, led the pre-seed portion of the raise. The Jobandtalent co-founders also joined, as did angel investors drawn from the legal and technology industries, among them executives at HappyRobot, Fuse Energy and several multinational banking and energy groups. Reversa also receives backing from Enisa and from the Neotec programme run by CDTI.

The newly introduced capital will help Reversa widen the international reach of its regulatory infrastructure and develop sector-focused products on top of it, targeting areas including financial services, energy and real estate. On the urban planning side, the firm is developing agents designed to streamline land-use permits, a recognised obstacle to building new homes. Hiring across engineering, product and sales is also planned.

In a recent development, reversa’s platform features a regulatory radar, through which agents link directly to official sources, assess how each regulatory change affects a business and support the steps needed to put it into practice. The technology also tackles operational and commercial challenges, such as pinpointing which legal framework applies when a organization enters a upcoming market, or automating compliance checks on a new product.

Sources indicate that customers also use it for jurisdiction-specific legal research and for drafting and revising contracts and policies. For public affairs teams, the agents track legislative procedures in real time, helping organisations prepare for upcoming rule changes and engage with the lawmaking process.

Great Lakes, which holds an A+ rating from AM Best, will provide the capacity, while ERGO Travel Insurance Services Ltd, part of Munich Re manufacturer ERGO Group, will oversee the arrangement as MGA under delegated authority from Great Lakes. All fresh business from 5 November 2026 falls under the partnership, and renewals will transfer from the same date.

The deal came after Great Lakes reviewed Napo’s underwriting proposition and business intends, and it gives the pet insurer long-term capacity supported by an A+ financial strength rating as it expands.

It has been revealed that alongside the capacity agreement, Napo has added new cover options underwritten by Great Lakes. Its lifetime range now includes 40 options, with yearly vet fee limits between £2,000 and £16,000, plus a choice of excess and co-pay.

Recent findings suggest that mercia Ventures, an existing backer, led the funding round. IW Capital and Advantage Insurance Organization Limited took part as new investors, and DN Capital and Companion Fund, the pet-care venture arm of Mars Petcare, made follow-on investments.

Sources indicate that the company did not disclose the size of the round. Napo plans to direct the capital towards further automation in pricing and claims and towards expanding its direct distribution.

Jean-Philippe Doumeng co-founded Napo in 2021 and named the company after his dachshund, Napoleon. He set it up because many pet owners do not realise how fast veterinary costs rise until their animal is sick or hurt, and by then it can be too late to buy a policy.

Sources indicate that napo handles pricing, claims and customer service in-house and applies AI where it makes cover fairer. Its machine-learning pricing models draw on the organization’s own policy and claims data, local vet costs and an AI-generated health profile covering more than 500 breeds. This approach lets Napo price rarer breeds on their individual traits instead of automatically classing them as high risk, and it can detect patterns such as how a dachshund’s risk shifts as it ages.

Tether, the largest company in the digital asset sector, has made an investment in Lemon, an Argentine FinTech focused on digital assets, in a bid to widen adoption of USD₮ and XAU₮ throughout Latin America.

The backing is intended to help Lemon create financial products built on digital assets that cost less and are simpler for customers to use.

The size of the investment was not disclosed.

In a recent development, the two firms blueprint to extend work Lemon has already been doing to make USD₮ and XAU₮ part of everyday financial activity. To keep things straightforward for customers, Lemon provides one Digital Dollar balance underpinned by USD₮.

In a recent development, the platform manages currencies, exchange rates and networks behind the scenes, leaving owners free to concentrate on spending, saving or transferring funds. Through XAU₮, customers can also put money into gold without needing a substantial initial sum, as tokenisation allows them to hold fractional amounts of gold that can be tracked and managed within the app.

Industry observers note that lemon operates an app that combines digital assets with day-to-day money management. Customers can save, generate yield, buy stocks, make and receive cross-border payments and, in markets where it is offered, pay using Visa prepaid virtual cards. The firm aims to give people access to their money at any time and in any place by cutting out needless steps between users and their funds.

Neem, a provider of unified financial infrastructure for businesses in Pakistan, has secured backing from ADB Ventures as part of its Pre-Series A round to expand its presence across the country.

In a recent development, the size of the investment from ADB Ventures, the venture capital arm of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), was not disclosed. Neem will use the capital to grow its financial infrastructure platform and lending portfolio, improve its product capabilities and reach more of the Pakistani market.

Several other investors joined the Pre-Series A round. These include DNI Group, HI2 Global, AKD Securities Limited, Epic Angels and the Pakistan Startup Fund. Strategic angel investors from PayNet, Aspire, Stripe and other international FinTech and payments companies also took part.

Neem’s lending offering includes earned wage access. This lets employees draw on wages they have already earned, with a particular focus on blue-collar workers in industries that employ large workforces. The service aims to give workers a responsible option and reduce their dependence on informal borrowing. The company also intends to offer financing to businesses. Merchants using its platform would be able to obtain working capital based on their transaction and settlement records, rather than only on conventional financial statements.

Neem’s platform brings together the tools businesses need to handle the flow of money. Clients can collect payments, send out funds, oversee balances, automate settlements and reconcile transactions in one place. The organization works with more than 70 enterprise customers in sectors including logistics, utilities, insurance, manufacturing and retail.

Sources indicate that the new funding marks the start of Neem’s next growth phase. The firm prepares to extend its digital financial rails to help businesses and the broader Pakistani economy continue to digitise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Industry observers note that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

According to recent reports, of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

According to recent reports, every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, when contact center agents speak to customers, they spend valuable time recording the information they need to solve the customer's problem in a step-by-step guide.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can use AI agents with step-by-step guides in the following AWS regions: US East (N.

AI agents in Amazon Connect Customer can now populate fields of a step-by-step guide for contact center agents during live customer interactions. With step-by-step guides, managers can design forms and other user interfaces for common workflows, such as rebooking a trip or submitting a claim. Now, AI agents can fill in a guide when it first loads and suggest updates during live conversations, saving time and improving data accuracy.

According to recent reports, when contact center agents speak to customers, they spend valuable time recording the information they need to solve the customer's problem in a step-by-step guide. For example, when a traveler calls an airline to change her flight, the agent might record her booking reference, dates of travel, and seat preferences. Now, Connect Customer's AI agents can automatically suggest and populate information like this, based on the context of the conversation. Human agents can review each suggestion, accept or reject suggestions individually or in bulk, and make any edits before submitting. The agent can focus on the customer and the problem at hand rather than on manual data entry.

Recent findings suggest that you can use AI agents with step-by-step guides in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker Studio now provides a native developer experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, enabling data scientists to submit distributed training jobs, deploy models, and monitor workloads through a visual interface on HyperPod clusters orchestrated with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built infrastructure for distributed training and fine-tuning of foundation models at scale, designed to reduce infrastructure management overhead. Submitting training jobs and deploying custom models on HyperPod at scale requires familiarity with kubectl and authoring Kubernetes manifests, creating operational burden for data scientists who prefer to work in an interactive development environment.

It has been revealed that with this launch, data scientists can now submit distributed PyTorch and Ray training jobs and deploy models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx, through single-page forms with a live YAML preview in SageMaker Studio. Compute configurations in the forms provide reusable resource presets that data scientists select when submitting training jobs or deploying models, eliminating manual compute entry. Metrics and logs are embedded directly in the detail pages, powered by HyperPod Observability and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, surfacing Kubernetes conditions and events, CloudWatch logs, and embedded metrics so data scientists can diagnose workloads without leaving their environment. For teams managing multiple workloads and using HyperPod task governance, Studio provides a unified queue view where consumers can see all pending tasks across training jobs and inference services, and adjust a task's priority class directly to optimize cluster utilization.

These updates are available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Amazon SageMaker Studio are currently supported.

To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod in Studio documentation.

#45189. Latest Update: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1755 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • It has been revealed that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

It has been revealed that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer aims the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

It has been revealed that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

In a recent development, we trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

According to recent reports, there's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

According to recent reports, every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and states why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

Sources indicate that "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

Sources indicate that "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

According to recent reports, the hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

Industry observers note that what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Sources indicate that users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

Recent findings suggest that the designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

Recent findings suggest that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

In a recent development, figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

According to recent reports, first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

It has been revealed that the key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

According to recent reports, figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

According to recent reports, to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

It has been revealed that presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

Sources indicate that the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

In a recent development, we also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4. To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing. To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vice President – IT & Cybersecurity, ALLEN Career Institute Pvt. Ltd.

Add advanced security protections on top of streamlined management with Chrome Enterprise Premium.

Sources indicate that editor’s note: Founded in 1988 in Kota, Rajasthan, ALLEN is one of India’s leading coaching institutions, serving over 400,000 students across 350+ classroom campuses in 78 cities. Here, the IT and Cybersecurity Leadership Team shares how they standardized on Chrome Enterprise Premium to secure sensitive data and enable zero trust across over 5,000 users.

According to recent reports, with a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ customers include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population.

According to recent reports, operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser.

The challenge of a fragmented browser estate.

We previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a newly introduced tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs.

Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise Premium.

In a recent development, we implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred consumers across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture.

The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity.

Recent findings suggest that the real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction.

In a recent development, with Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console.

Industry observers note that we use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts.

Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • According to recent reports, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

According to recent reports, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

According to recent reports, however, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

Industry observers note that A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that rapidly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Sources indicate that say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

According to recent reports, either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a latest 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

According to recent reports, all three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

Sources indicate that this is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

According to recent reports, SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

According to recent reports, on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

Recent findings suggest that A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

According to recent reports, getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

Sources indicate that we confirmed Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

In a recent development, phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

According to recent reports, the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Sources indicate that developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

It has been revealed that we built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

In a recent development, phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It has been revealed that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Recent findings suggest that phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a fresh one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

Recent findings suggest that we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

According to recent reports, phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

According to recent reports, one line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly reveals where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud.

  • According to recent reports, today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President, Google Cloud Platform & SRE.

According to recent reports, for over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

According to recent reports, today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:.

It has been revealed that workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

According to recent reports, google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Industry observers note that together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:.

Sources indicate that policy checks on every request: Under our latest Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

Recent findings suggest that people stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and owners will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

According to recent reports, boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and owners to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

In a recent development, strict rules on your data afterward: Our newly introduced Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your owners, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

Recent findings suggest that with Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.
