#45144. Industry News: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6149 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • Recent findings suggest that open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • Sources indicate that the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Recent findings suggest that open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

Sources indicate that the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

Recent findings suggest that in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

According to recent reports, AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

According to recent reports, lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, confirmed in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

According to recent reports, with the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

Industry observers note that we work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel highlights what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Industry observers note that starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no latest work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

It has been revealed that adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

In a recent development, figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

In a recent development, model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Sources indicate that public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material problems in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

According to recent reports, similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

According to recent reports, for example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Sources indicate that the SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

It has been revealed that however, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

In a recent development, balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Industry observers note that table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Sources indicate that our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

Sources indicate that in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

Recent findings suggest that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a new harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

That is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Recent findings suggest that consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 indicates the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Industry observers note that table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

Sources indicate that for the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

According to recent reports, the model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote latest instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Industry observers note that the D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Sources indicate that figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

In a recent development, before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Industry observers note that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

Recent findings suggest that it is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Sources indicate that several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

According to recent reports, finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to newly introduced spectra.

Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

Recent findings suggest that when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Recent findings suggest that inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each upcoming model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

It has been revealed that figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

In a recent development, the comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

It has been revealed that reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Industry observers note that environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no fresh work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each newly introduced task.

In a recent development, evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The upcoming work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Industry observers note that evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

Recent findings suggest that no-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

It has been revealed that terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Recent findings suggest that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

According to recent reports, agentic evaluations are important for understanding how reliably AI agents perform across different tasks and scenarios. I think AI agent observability is equally valuable because tracking an agent’s behavior, decisions, and performance helps identify challenges and improve results over time. This is also relevant to practical business applications such as automated customer verification, as discussed here: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-kyc-automation-customer-verification.

Industry observers note that amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports managed cluster extensions for Slurm clusters. You can install, configure, update, and remove managed features through the SageMaker AI console or API. The first two extensions cover observability and user management. Earlier, every observability or user management change for HyperPod Slurm clusters meant editing lifecycle scripts and then replacing or rerunning nodes. Now, HyperPod manages these features for you, and you keep lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs for your organization's own software.

According to recent reports, for each extension, you declare a configuration. HyperPod validates it and applies it to every node, including nodes you add later. It then reports the extension's status and the health of each node. The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), Slurm job, and Slurm cluster metrics. It sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and you can add Amazon Managed Grafana dashboards. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node. It also controls who can sign in with SSH and use sudo on each node type, with local users, Active Directory, or both.

Sources indicate that cluster extensions are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available. You pay only for the AWS resources you use. To learn more, see Cluster extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide, read the launch blog, or visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

According to recent reports, AI has intensified investors' interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered "signals" that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

According to recent reports, as agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

Industry observers note that their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?

Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue.

According to recent reports, this yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little?

Sources indicate that by reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children's developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap.

Latest Update: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models.
  • One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture.
  • Industry observers note that we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

Industry observers note that we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):.

bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:.

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

It has been revealed that speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:.

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:.

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):.

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

There is Dflash2 for it already.Quite a bit faster.

Industry observers note that AWS Sign-In now enables developers and AI agents to stay authenticated for up to 90 days without frequent sign-ins or consent prompts. With this launch, administrators can configure Sign-in duration, which controls how long an OAuth Sign-in session remains active, for individual IAM consumers and roles.

Sources indicate that this capability reduces authentication interruptions for long-running workflows and provides a more secure alternative to static access keys by using short-lived, renewable credentials. Existing session duration limits remain unchanged unless administrators explicitly configure longer durations.

Sign-In Duration supports AWS CLI (aws login), AWS MCP Server, and other OAuth-enabled applications. It does not affect AWS Management Console sessions. Customers can configure the setting using the IAM console, AWS CLI, or IAM API in all AWS commercial Regions.

To learn more, see the AWS Sign-In session management User Guide, Configure Sign-In duration on Role User Guide, Condition Key User Guide.

#45139. How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (712 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas.
  • Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries.
  • Sources indicate that just one example: Aims for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Sources indicate that just one example: Aims for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

Recent findings suggest that if you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build upcoming energy capacity today.

Sources indicate that but there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

According to recent reports, PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

Sources indicate that this AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The firm mentioned that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not fresh for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

It has been revealed that but the desire to come online swiftly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

Breaking: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English.
  • We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness.
  • Sources indicate that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

Sources indicate that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

According to recent reports, CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

It has been revealed that the key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

Sources indicate that because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

Industry observers note that adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Sources indicate that search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

According to recent reports, the fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

In a recent development, you do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

In a recent development, nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

In a recent development, voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

Recent findings suggest that this approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

According to recent reports, this is an interesting example of how voice agents can support Indic languages and make AI more accessible to diverse consumers. I think AI agent cost optimization is also worth considering when developing voice-based solutions, as managing compute resources and usage costs can help make these applications more practical to scale. X8i instances come in 14 sizes, from large to 96xlarge, including two bare metal options.

#45136. The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1810 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager.
  • In a recent development, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm.
  • The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

In a recent development, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows people to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

It has been revealed that researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

Recent findings suggest that the accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, notes Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”.

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

It has been revealed that the hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

It has been revealed that davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”.

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

According to recent reports, nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, indicates George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

In a recent development, to get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, indicates George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”.

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” notes George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

Recent findings suggest that at first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” indicates Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”.

Recent findings suggest that davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.

According to recent reports, today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also states he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” claims Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology tech giant that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

Sources indicate that the research team is right now planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” indicates Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Industry observers note that davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he claims.

George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he claims. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”.

Recent findings suggest that davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he states. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”.

#45135. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
