📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been cooking dinner for myself (and/or my family) nearly every night for the past 27 years. Suffice it to say I've learned some kitchen tips and tricks during those decades—especially about what is and isn't worth taking up valuable counter space.

Some of my favorite kitchen gadgets may not be the most flashy (a measuring cup, a mesh cloth, a cast-iron pan). Instead, they're the kinds of things that really matter when you cook a lot, whether in service of keeping things clean and organized, or sharp, or preserving your hard work by freezing leftovers for a future busy night.

I've also thrown in a couple of fun nice-to-haves, including a kit for making Giada De Laurentiis' viral (and highly recommended!) sheet-pan lasagna and a 500-piece puzzle that may send you on a soup-making side quest.

For more gift ideas, check out our Best Gifts Under $100, Best Tech Gifts, and Best Gifts Under $25.

In a recent development, if your giftee loves baking sourdough but hates having to feed their starter every day or revive it every time it goes in the fridge, this could be a game-changing device—it was for me. It requires some futzy calibration and adjustment at first, but I've kept my starter going and in a ready-to-use state for almost a month with this handy gadget that works for any type of flour.

It has been revealed that cast iron cookware is unparalleled for its heat retention, durability, and nonstick nature, so long as you keep it well seasoned. But it's also heavy and often difficult to maneuver. You could always use lightweight carbon steel, made with an iron-carbon alloy, but it doesn't really act like cast iron in that it's highly variable in terms of heat. Field's heirloom-quality pans are modeled on smooth vintage designs and are just as lightweight as stainless steel, yet retain all the benefits of cast iron. WIRED operations manager Scott Gilberston likes them a lot, and so do I.

It has been revealed that even though I cook every day, I'm terrible at sharpening knives. I never feel like I'm doing it correctly on the manual honing rods or pull-through sharpeners, but with this electric model, I found success. There's still a learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, you'll be able to sharpen a whole block's worth of knives in about half an hour. I was even able to revive a chef's knife that hadn't been sharpened in nearly 20 years, sitting dull and forgotten at the back of a drawer.

In a recent development, after I lived in Mexico for a year, I became unable to eat store-bought tortillas. Sure, they're easy, with no preparation required beyond warming them. But they're also limp, flavorless, sad little excuses for food. Alternatively, homemade tortillas are things of beauty and exemplify what I love about cooking: using simple, high-quality ingredients to produce something far better than you would expect. Fortunately, making your own tortillas is incredibly easy—well, if you have a tortilla press, and the best I've used is this one from Masienda, which nicely offers the ability to press larger tortillas.

If your foodie friend likes Mexican food, this gift will expand their culinary horizons. The combo pack provides everything they need to get started on making their own tortillas: masa and a press. The key to great homemade tortillas is great masa harina, and Masienda's flour is my favorite (well, outside of Mexico anyway). —Scott Gilbertson.

Industry observers note that look, we’re major fans at WIRED of the viral (and manly) Männkitchen pepper mill and its 50 grind settings, but its plain black basic-peppermill look isn’t exactly giftable. HexMill's HexClad burr-grinder pepper mill is pretty darn close in terms of performance, with 10 grind settings and a lifetime warranty. Plus, it comes in four anodized aluminum colors that make it feel special and personalized. I also like that it holds up to half a cup of peppercorns—more than any other pepper mill I've tried. I've been using one of these almost daily for the past few months and haven't had to refill it yet.

According to recent reports, who doesn't love a quick and easy sheet-pan meal? If you haven’t yet tried making Giada De Laurentiis’ viral sheet-pan lasagna, you should. This kit allows your giftee to make it just as the celebrity chef intended, with purée made from hand-picked tomatoes in Salerno, Italy; organic olive oil from Coratina; a custom salt blend; and a box of taccole cut in Abruzzo on 100-year-old bronze dies.

In a recent development, you'll need to buy the perishables, like ricotta, sausage, and vegetables. But the recipe is worth the extra spend, considering how much food the kit makes; the description says six servings, but it could easily feed double that if you throw in a side salad. Note that the included recipe is a bit vague on equipment, but to prepare the sausage and onions, you'll need a 14-inch pan; my 12-incher was not big enough.

According to recent reports, this gift is a great mix of beauty and utility. Many of my cook friends already have serious affection for All-Clad's set of measuring spoons ($35), which are preciously shaped not like spoons but like miniature All-Clad pans—a visual pun that also makes small measures of spices or flour much easier to parse visually than you could with a spoon-shaped spoon.

This set is even more special—and useful. It includes the odd and vexing sizes that nonetheless turn up constantly in baking recipes: 1.5 teaspoons or 1.5 cups, a ¾ cup or a ⅔ cup. These are measurements that often require eyeballing or using multiple measuring cups to achieve. Any cook, and especially any baker, who receives this gift will feel both charmed and understood. —Matthew Korfhage.

It has been revealed that even before the advent of the Gen Z aesthetic police (no offense; I live with one) and ASMR “restock my pantry” reels, there's been something irresistible about a perfectly organized set of spices. Evermill's has been popular for a while, and for good reason—there's no kitchen where this sleek black (or white, silver, or gunmetal) rack wouldn't look good.

Recent findings suggest that and these aren't your typical spice jars prefilled with dusty, flavorless grounds, either. You'll get to pick which ones you want, and they're fresh and organic and come in resealable bags so you can add as much or as little as you want at a time.

As former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage has mentioned, “Every cook has seen these checkerboard-looking cutting boards and thirsted for them a little.” No lies detected. The handsome look comes from end-grain pieces for a more durable surface. It's a hefty board that's intended to be out in your kitchen full time, not tucked away in a cabinet. Korfhage had the walnut version, but I have the maple version, which is a little cheaper but still showstopping.

It has been revealed that thirty-five Southeast Asian noodle dishes—including pho, bun bo hue, noodle plates, fish ball soups, and more—form a colorful mosaic in this 500-piece puzzle. Visual artist and world traveler Troy Litten photographed (and ate!) all the plates featured. It's a fun gift for any puzzle-loving foodie or world traveler you know. I lent it to two people who tend to prefer puzzles of at least 1,000 pieces, and they still loved this one, finding it challenging enough to hold their interest.

It has been revealed that A vacuum sealer has always been one of my most-used kitchen appliances, for both sous vide cooking and sealing large-batch leftovers. The vacuum sealer I owned, a FoodSaver, was massive and cost more than $200 at the time. This Fresko model is small enough to fit in a cabinet (roughly 16 inches long by 8 inches wide) and also comes with a roll of food-safe, cut-to-fit bags and 10 pre-cut bags that are perfect for most items. I've used the Fresko for both wet goods like marinated meats, and dry like frozen blocks of sauces and leftovers (made with Souper Cubes, below). No matter the item, I've never had any issues getting a good seal.

Industry observers note that instant-read thermometers are something every cook should have. It might be cool to saunter over to the grill and gently prod your steak with a finger and pronounce it medium well, but few of us can reliably do that. The Thermapen One will tell you the exact internal temperature in one second. No need for elaborate guesswork.

Cheap instant-read thermometers litter Amazon, but we like the more expensive Thermapen One for its reliability (mine is five years old and still going strong) and speed. Yes, speed really does matter, because the longer the oven is open or the grill lid is off, the more it cools and the more unevenly you end up cooking. Get them the best thermometer, and you'll guarantee they'll temp your hanger steak exactly the way you like it. —Scott Gilbertson.

Many cooks put a lot of time and effort into making not only meals but things that make the meals—stocks, broths, sauces, chopped vegetables, beans. I have been obsessed with Souper Cubes for years, as they allow me to freeze my hard work for later, as well as preserve about-to-go-bad store-bought sauces, salsas, and even tomato paste in specific increments like half-cups, tablespoons, or even one- or two-cup blocks. I then like to vacuum seal them, but you can also just put the cubes in a zip-lock bag. There are cheaper versions of these out there, but Souper Cubes have steel wire inside so they won't crush, sag, or crumple, plus their lids let you stack them in the freezer.

According to recent reports, if you’re a baker, especially of long doughs like pizza and bread, you’re likely all too familiar with the difficulty of cleaning bowls, mixers, starter containers, and any other surface that touched sticky, developed gluten. It doesn’t take much for sponges—or sinks, or pipes—to become entombed in the stuff, sometimes intractably. The answer is the Keeki Cloth, a square of webbed polyester mesh that cleans even the biggest baking messes effectively and immediately. Best of all, it’s machine washable, so you can thoroughly clean and sanitize it before its next use.

It has been revealed that I’ve been using—and machine-washing—mine for over a year, and it still looks good as latest. In fact, I love it so much, I often use it with dish soap to clean regular dishes of stuck-on food. A three-pack is just $15, making it an easy stocking stuffer, hostess gift, or reason to keep a few in rotation.

Recent findings suggest that aarke's Carbonator 3 lives full-time on my kitchen counter, mainly for cocktails and making my own sparkling-water concoctions. But adding sparkling water to batter for tempura and waffles is a known hack to make them lighter and crispier, so the machine could also double as a chef's tool. I also appreciate that it uses no electricity, so you don't need to situate it near an outlet. This retro appliance is a showpiece in any color option, but Aarke gilded the lily with a new line of vintage-inspired shades this year, including textured Heritage Green (shown) and Burgundy.

According to recent reports, no herb garden in December? No problem. I keep herbs in my kitchen year-round thanks to the Auk, which is one of the most thoughtfully designed indoor hydroponic garden setups I've ever used. It comes with parsley and basil seeds, but you can grow anything you want in the coco coir pots, as well as adjust light schedules and initiate vacation mode (which dims the lights for slower growth) in the easy-to-use app. The mid-century-inspired Scandinavian design is a bonus.

Recent findings suggest that turn the downside of cooking—doing dishes—into an upside with a thoughtfully designed dish rack. I know few people with a truly functional dish rack situation, and this is the best one I have ever owned. It's got a little tower for wine glasses and a tray for small items like gaskets and caps. The best part may just be the bottom that slopes into a spout that drains right back into the sink. No more moldy, wet drying mats or water dripping onto the floor.

I use steak knives for a lot more than meat—bread, produce, cutting sandwiches in half, even opening packages in a pinch—which means my steak knives often end up in rough shape, making for a sad complement on the table when I actually do make steaks for company or even just my family. A set of “good” steak knives is something your cooking giftee may not bother buying for themself, but I highly recommend having it. This Anolon set is my favorite, as there are no plastic or wooden handles to weather or discolor, and the knives have a good weight to them.

#45056. Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk.
  • That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”.

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Sources indicate that yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

It has been revealed that at the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”.

Recent findings suggest that pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” noted Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”.

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma remarked. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”.

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

Sources indicate that in 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Upcoming York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

Sources indicate that “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”.

Sources indicate that according to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.

It has been revealed that gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines noted, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

According to recent reports, pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a fresh $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very major support network outside of my friends.”.

One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying latest stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines stated.

When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they promptly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

Sources indicate that “ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”.

Industry observers note that another volunteer, Lew Lefton, mentioned he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends,” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”.

Sources indicate that back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

According to recent reports, “The beauty of it,” Pettus mentioned, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”.

Industry observers note that around this time, unbeknownst to Swan, his name went on Sequoiaâs list of âprefoundersâ to keep an eye on, thanks to Edward OâCarroll, a former talent lead at Sequoia. âWe have a term called âdynamoâ at Sequoia for people who are slightly earlier in their careers, but we would describe them as very high slope in terms of their rate of evolution,â states George Robson, a partner at Sequoia who wrapped up his own time at Revolut in 2020. âMark was put on this list for exactly that reason â he was a âdynamo.ââ.

Sources indicate that confident in their product, the Nevis co-founders approached their Sequoia partners with a go-to-market blueprint centered on the U.K. Robson and Lixandru challenged them, however, to look at other, larger markets where AI is more rapidly being deployed. In a recent development, nevisâs decision to come out of stealth mode is a result of the momentum itâs seeing in the U.S. âWe have enormous market demand,â Swan notes, âand whatâs more, we have validation from current customers around the strength of our product. It continues to attract those who cut their teeth at Revolut; many of Nevisâs current employees, like its co-founders, are alumni of the manufacturer. Swan, Burda and Chalov recognize that people â from the internal team at Nevis, to the wealth management firms that use their product, to the clients depending on trusted advisors for wealth management â are the key to the companyâs success. This is more true than ever right now, as we seem to be in a liminal period; animal spirits have lulled, but AI companies continue to put up strong results.

My prediction for 2026 is that it will be a tale of two AIs. On the one hand, it will be a year of delays, first in data center buildouts, many of which will fall behind schedule, and second, in the AGI timeline. At the same time, AI adoption will continue its relentless rise. In 2025, startups coined the idea of a â$0 to $100Mâ club of rapidly scaling AI companies; in 2026, weâll begin to talk about the â$0 to $1Bâ club.

Entering 2026, here are the facts as I see them:.

Demand for AI CapEx from the Major Tech companies is stronger than ever.

Google and Meta are fully betting the farm on AI.

While Microsoft and Amazon pulled back slightly in 2025 relative to peers, both continue to aggressively position themselves for the AI future.

According to recent reports, supply chain players seem weary: The customerâs customer is not as healthy as theyâd wish. They are worried about being left holding the bag.

The end revenue from AI remains limited (on the order of tens of billions per year) relative to the scale of data center and energy investments (on the order of trillions over the coming five years).

It has been revealed that there are two killer apps in AI, coding and ChatGPT. Both are expected to approach or cross double digit billions of revenue this year. Nearly a dozen more startups are on the path to cross $100M+ in the near future, across a wide variety of applications.

Major enterprises are struggling to implement AI in-house, which is leading to fatigue and disappointment.

These countervailing forces will collide in 2026: soaring Big Tech demand will run headfirst into a supply chain that hasnât scaled fast enough to match it.

According to recent reports, first, companies like TSMC and ASML have monopolistic positions and cannot be forced to ramp capacity. Ben Thompson has called this the âTSMC Brake,â pointing out in October that while TSMC had ramped revenues by 50% since 2022, they had only ramped CapEx by 10%. He explained further: âThere werenât too many answers from TSMC about this, which is understandable, given that they wonât announce next yearâs CapEx numbers until next quarter. What Wei did say is that TSMC was making a point to not just talk to its customers but its customersâ customers.â My prediction, especially coming off of the successful Gemini 3 launch and hype around TPUs, is that the TSMC constraint could become material in 2026.

According to recent reports, second, industrial players, which tend to be overlooked due to their fragmentation and lack of market power, may end up creating bottlenecks as data centers move into the final stages of construction. Generators and cooling units are among the most important industrial inputs to data centers, but there are dozens of such inputs; if any of these inputs are delayed, timelines would need to be pushed out. There are also labor constraints that must be factored in, as shortages in skilled labor could become a key bottleneck for completing these immense construction projects. Many AI companies share a supply base, and these industrial suppliers are faced with their own CapEx decisions (how many new factories to build). Weâll find out in 2026 to what extent theyâve sufficiently added to their own output capacity.

According to recent reports, the average AI data center takes roughly two years to build. So if 2024 was the year of new project announcements, and 2025 was the year when construction investments started to hit GDP, then 2026 will either be the year where a lot of this new capacity comes online (leading to further declines in the cost of compute) or it will be the year when many of these construction projects begin to face delays. We already have seen a few of these delays publicly reported in Q4 2025. If hyperscalers begin to warehouse their new AI chips rather than installing them directly into data centers, this will be a telltale sign that the era of delays has begun.

According to recent reports, the other way in which 2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ has to do with the AGI timeline. For a long time, Silicon Valley luminaries were forecasting the imminent emergence of AGI, with âAGI in 2027â thrown around frequently in conversation. Since June of this year, there has been a progressive walk-back of this timeline. Dwarkesh Patelâs recent podcast interviews with Richard Sutton, Andrej Karpathy, and Ilya Sutskever are a demarcating line; the new consensus is that the AGI window will be in the 2030s, at earliest. In the coming year, I expect this âupdateâ to filter outside of Silicon Valley. There are implications across many areas. The most notable risk is that hyperscaler CapEx today ends up being outdated.

Tale 2: The Relentless Drive Toward AI Adoption.

In a recent development, the area where I do not expect to see any delays is in AI adoption itself. The fading of hype will have little impact on fundamentals. If anything, the best startups are growing faster than ever from $0 to $100M in revenue. In 2026, weâre going to see the emergence of a $0 to $1B club. The trend of the last three yearsâand likely for many moreâis that startups are laying the foundation for the future economy, one building block at a time. There are many excellent entrepreneurs exploring upcoming niches, and a lot of latent value has yet to be unlocked.

It has been revealed that the best AI startups are moving with extreme efficiencyâmany are earning north of $1M in revenue per employee. This implies market pull vs. a push sale. Todayâs entrepreneurs are building âself-improvingâ companiesâthey are themselves using AI agents for functions like legal, recruiting, and salesâcreating an ecosystem flywheel effect. AI app companies are also riding a compute cost curve that should drive incremental margin improvement, especially as fresh data centers come online between now and 2030. Finally, with enterprises facing adoption fatigue on DIY implementations, startups are gaining even more momentum.

For some, AI adoption is happening too slowly. Those expecting a rapid AI takeoff would prefer to see a deus ex machina moment carry us straight to the finish line. I think that dream is likely to disappoint. Instead, the next leg of the AI story will require hard work, creative brilliance, and endurance to reach a newly introduced threshold where AI radically transforms the economy. We need only to look at the green shootsâfounder motivation, aggressiveness, hunger to win, customer obsessionâto see that this future is coming.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that netflix recently entered into a definitive agreement to buy Warner Brothers for over $82B in Enterprise Value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Recent findings suggest that netflix recently entered into a definitive agreement to buy Warner Brothers for over $82B in Enterprise Value. Itâs being called the biggest, most consequential deal in Hollywood history. The purchase comes with intellectual property including Batman, Superman, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Substantial Bang Theory, The Sopranos, The Matrix, Lord of the Rings (film rights), Godzilla/MonsterVerse, Mad Max, and Mortal Kombat.

IP like this became more valuable in the internet age, and will become even more valuable in the age of AI. Earlier this year, I published an internal Sequoia memo detailing the implications of AI on the IP industry. Given the big news, I thought it would be nice to share a few excerpts with my friends and colleagues more broadly.

On a recent work trip to Paris, a profound irony struck me at the MusÃ©e dâOrsay. The museum, a glorious former train station, is a temple to the Industrial Revolution. Its collection, spanning 1848 to 1914, chronicles the period of historyâs most rapid industrialization.

Edgar Degas: Course de Gentleman (Gentlemenâs Race).

Industry observers note that the art is filled with tributes to this newly introduced age: Monet paints locomotives at La Gare Saint-Lazare, smokestacks fill the background of Degasâ Course de Gentlemen, and the Traders in factory-made clothing. It is a museum drenched in the dawn of industrialization.

Claude Monet: La Gare Saint-Lazare.

It has been revealed that this is where the paradox lies. This was the exact moment in history when the cost to reproduce a piece of art dropped precipitously. What was once near-impossible, replicating a masterpiece, became trivially cheap. Logically, as near-perfect copies became ubiquitous, the value of the âoriginalâ should have plummeted. And yet, the opposite happened. The great lesson of the dâOrsay is this: instead of becoming worthless in the age of manufacturing, these original works became priceless. As reproduction became easy, the value and allure of the original only went up.

Edgar Degas: At the Stock Exchange.

Hereâs why IP is well positioned in an AI future:.

If we have AGI, or even inexpensive content creation, that will drive down the cost of intelligence.

That affordable intelligence will be used to create an abundance of content.

Humans will react to abundance with a desire for familiarity and quality.

The value of the âoriginalâ will only increase.

In this era, âoriginalâ works will increase in value quickly.

These âoriginalsâ include art, real estate, and intellectual property.

Intellectual property that has already earned a spot in our minds will benefit disproportionately.

In the AI Era, nostalgic content will benefit disproportionately as it is manifest in countless different ways.

In a recent development, as content production costs approach zero, the marginal cost of new content will also become negligible, leading to an explosion in content volume. This content flood will profoundly shift the value of attention, the primary currency in this new landscape. Undifferentiated content will rapidly lose value, and consumers will be far less willing to invest time in new content unless itâs algorithmically recommended by dominant platforms. Very few new content concepts will break out, following an extreme Power Law.

Success in this environment will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent interest in a specific piece of content. Nostalgic content is poised to become the most valuable. In a world saturated with novelty, authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly difficult to simulate accurately; even slight deviations from the original will feel inauthentic and cheap.

Industry observers note that consumers will be willing to pay for nostalgic content due to its relatively low cost. For parents, the decision to purchase authentic nostalgic content for their children over a knockoff, especially when the real item is priced reasonably, becomes a clear choice.

The Impending Content Deluge and the Scarcity of Attention.

Industry observers note that the ubiquity of General AI will drastically reduce the marginal cost of content production, approaching zero. This will unleash an unprecedented explosion in content volume, creating a hyper-saturated information environment. In this landscape, human attention, rather than content itself, will become the primary scarce resource and the dominant currency. Undifferentiated content, easily replicable and ubiquitous, will rapidly depreciate in value. Consumers, overwhelmed by choice, will increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendations from dominant content platforms to filter and curate their experiences, leading to a profound shift in content discovery and consumption patterns.

Attention Distribution: The Latest Competitive Moat.

Success in this AI-driven content economy will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent and deeply ingrained interest in a specific piece of content. This is distinct from mere algorithmic visibility, as it speaks to an intrinsic desire to engage with content. While AI can generate novel content at scale, it will struggle to replicate the nuanced emotional resonance and deeply embedded cultural references that drive genuine attention.

The Inherent Value of Authentic Nostalgic Content.

Industry observers note that nostalgic content is uniquely positioned to become the most valuable asset in this future. The core arguments for its enduring value are:.

Difficulty of Authentic Simulation: While AGI can mimic styles and tropes, accurately simulating authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly challenging. The most popular feature in Sora 2 is their âCameoâ feature, which pulls in authentic characters and people into the AI generated worlds. Even minute deviations from the original, like a slight alteration in a beloved characterâs voice, a subtle anachronism in a period piece, or a deviation in the execution of a well-known narrative, will register as âinauthenticâ or âcheapâ to a discerning audience. The emotional connection to nostalgic content is often rooted in precise, well-remembered details, making it highly resistant to imperfect algorithmic replication. This is akin to the âuncanny valleyâ in robotics, where near-human but imperfect simulations evoke discomfort rather than acceptance.

Consumer Willingness to Pay: Despite the approaching zero marginal cost of content, consumers will demonstrate a significant willingness to pay for authentic nostalgic content.

Recent findings suggest that as AI democratizes content creation, the landscape will shift dramatically. The true scarcity will be human attention, and the ultimate value will reside in content that can capture and hold that attention through genuine emotional resonance. Authentic nostalgic content, by virtue of its irreplicable emotional depth and its proven ability to connect across generations, represents a highly defensible and appreciating asset in this evolving digital economy. Investors should prioritize companies that control and strategically leverage these invaluable cultural touchstones.

The inside feels soft and cozy, and the outside is rigid enough that I'd be happy throwing this into a carry-on.

This slim case gives a bit of protection and includes Joy-Con grips for added comfort. You can get different colors and your Switch 2 can still fit in dock with the case on, though it may be a tight squeeze.

The official Nintendo Switch 2 controllers are pricey and they don't have Pokémon on them, like this one does. There are also magnetic Hall effect thumbsticks that should be more durable than the joysticks found in other controllers, and programmable buttons on the rear to bind shortcuts to these easier-to-reach spots.

The 256 GB in your Switch 2 won't last long, so why not double it with this handy microSD card? This card works well, so it's worth grabbing while it's on sale.

In a recent development, IT is one of the most critical functions inside any company. Every employee depends on it, every system flows through it, and almost every operational challenge eventually becomes an IT problem. When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out fresh tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Recent findings suggest that yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business owners. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

It has been revealed that jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

According to recent reports, the second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

According to recent reports, these insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

According to recent reports, serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

At the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

Sources indicate that while their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Sources indicate that customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Many customers have already fully ripped and replaced incumbent ITSM tools and now use Serval as their system of record.

It has been revealed that automation quickly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

At Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

The market thesis is one half of the story. The other half is the team. References for Jake and Alex â from managers, direct reports, and peers â were glowing. Even more importantly, those references aligned perfectly with the evidence we heard from customers and what weâve observed in talent flows. Strong talent from R&D to GTM is choosing to join Serval, whether or not they have worked with the founders before. The talent density and âpotential energyâ forming around the manufacturer are impressive and represent one of the strongest leading indicators we look for.

Recent findings suggest that empowering IT teams is an elegant and scalable way to bring AI automation to the enterprise. We are excited to partner with Jake, Alex, and the team at Serval on this journey.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • From casual, everyday T-shirts, to underwear, socks, and great merino travel pants, Unbound has a little something for everyone.
  • Merino wool is great because you're stealing a sheep's ability to keep itself warm or cool based on the temperatures it's in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that merino Wool May be a super fiber well worth owning, but it isn't cheap. Right now, one of my favorite merino wool companies, Unbound Merino, is having its once-a-year sale. Unbound Merino's Black Friday sale is a great chance to round out your travel wardrobe with some excellent merino wool. Better hurry though, unlike most sales this time of year, Unbound Merino's Black Friday sale ends tonight.

From casual, everyday T-shirts, to underwear, socks, and great merino travel pants, Unbound has a little something for everyone. We've combed through the site and found a few of our favorite deals. Be sure to see our guide to the Best Merino Wool T-shirts, Best Merino Wool Clothes, and the Best Base Layers for more great merino wool options.

What’s So Great About Merino Wool?

Merino wool is great because you're stealing a sheep's ability to keep itself warm or cool based on the temperatures it's in. This is a process often referred to as thermoregulation. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool than what most people think of when they think of wool. The sheep evolved this soft coat to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures. The result is a fabric that's comfortable to wear next to your skin. For the softest tees, look for fabrics that are either superfine or ultrafine—anything 17 µm or higher—like Unbound's T-shirts.

Wool is sustainable, too. One sheep can produce 4 to 5 pounds of wool per year. While cotton has its place, and so does the occasional synthetic garment, merino wool is a remarkable fabric that's the cornerstone of my wardrobe. I don't think you can have too many merino pieces in your closet, but they’re not cheap, which is why we're featuring these deals.

What’s So Great About Unbound Merino?

I like Unbound's T-shirts because they're 100 percent merino wool, no synthetics involved. That means all the antibacterial, odor-resistant, moisture-wicking, temperature-regulating goodness of merino wool … just works. I've found Unbound's T-shirts in particular to be very quick-drying and wrinkle resistant, two of the reasons I think they're the best merino T-shirts for travel. The tech giant's pants also have a very high wool percentage (95 percent), and they roll up nicely, making them very packable. Do you need special travel clothing? No, but Unbound's merino wool is naturally odor-resistant, which means you need fewer pieces in your bag. The company also offers a 30-day guarantee. If you don't like it, you can send it back.

Recent findings suggest that most merino products come with care instructions. Unbound Merino's T-shirts should be washed cold with like colors, then laid flat to dry. Whatever you do, don't bleach them and don't tumble dry them. The latter is especially destructive. I do it to every wool T-shirt I test, and it makes me sad, but I know some of you won't listen and will do it anyway, so I have to know what happens so I can warn you. Don't tumble dry. Just put it on a drying rack. It doesn't take more than a day. Seriously, you just spent $80 (on sale!) on a T-shirt; take care of it. Properly cared for, high-quality merino clothing like Unbound's is incredibly durable and will last for years. Throw it in the dryer and the pilling starts almost immediately.

According to recent reports, do I always lay them flat to dry? No. When traveling I usually hand-wash in the sink and then drape them over the shower curtain rod to dry, which hasn't seemed to have much negative impact. The problems with hanging wool to dry is that it will stretch out from the water weight. This is particularly true with 100 percent merino, like Unbound's T-shirts.

In a recent development, I've never had a problem storing merino in my closet between wears, but for long-term storage, I recommend you take precautions against moths, which are notorious for eating holes in wool. I have lost merino garments to moths. I make sure to wash and thoroughly dry whatever I am storing, then I seal it in a compression bag. Another option is to put your merino garment in a cotton bag or otherwise wrap it in cotton and then put it in a plastic bin. It's very crucial to make sure that the garment is completely dry before using any of these storage methods; otherwise your wool will smell musty and moldy. Other options include storing your garment in a cedar chest, which is a good natural deterrent for moths, or use moth traps or lavender sachets, which will repel the moths.

Unbound Merino (Unbound Merino Women’s).

In a recent development, unbound's T-shirts were my introduction to the brand, and they're still one of my favorite merino T-shirts. This T-shirt is incredibly soft, and because it's 100 percent merino wool, it'll stay odor-free for ages—as long as five or six days in my testing (depending on local temps, what you're doing, etc). Unbound's crew neck merino T-shirt has a relaxed, casual cut. It's not going for the technical look you'll get from many outdoor brands. It's also lightweight and packs down to a tiny ball, which is perfect if you're looking to simplify down to one bag. (Really, is there any other way to travel?).

Sources indicate that the final thing I love about these is how fast they dry. In most climates, you can give it a wash in the sink at night, roll it up in a towel, wring it dry, lay it out flat, and it'll be dry by morning. If they have a downside, it's that Unbound's T-shirts do need to be babied a little. To help them last a long time I recommend hand washing and line-drying. Also note that while I like the merino crew neck, the V-neck is also on sale for $88 ($10 off).

In a recent development, unbound's merino travel pants are a light and comfortable merino blend, with plenty of stretch and freedom of moment, thanks to the 5 percent elastane. These have a more formal look, what you might call slacks if you are a certain type of person. You might even be able to pull off going to office in them, but I'd sooner chew my leg off than work in an office, so I don't really know. I can say I've worn them to nice restaurants without a second look, and yet they don't scream “I've got money” when you're stumbling back to your hotel room in Prague at 4 am.

In a recent development, as you would expect from anything Unbound makes, these pack down fantastically small. You can pack two pairs of these for every pair of jeans. Again, for serious travelers looking to live out of a single carry-on bag, that's huge. The only downside is that these are on the thin side, not something you'd want to wear alone in cold climates. If you're like me and have to deal with winter, throw a good base layer underneath them and you'll be fine. The slim fit pant is also on sale if that's more your style.

One of the best ways to save at the Unbound Merino Black Friday sale is to go for a bundle. I like this 1-Pack bundle, which gets you a T-shirt, underwear and socks for $125. There are quite a few other bundles as well, including the T-shirt 3-pack for $240 ($54 off) which is $20 cheaper than buying three T-shirts on sale, the boxer briefs pack for $75 ($15 off), and the sock 3-pack which is a steal at just $40 ($38 off).

In a recent development, unbound's merino boxers are warm without being hot, great at wicking moisture, and capable of several wears without undue odors. 84 percent merino wool, 12 percent nylon, and 4 percent spandex, for a soft, stretchy, comfortable fit. They're 180 GSM (see our merino guide for exactly what GSM means), which makes them nice and light. The inseam here is 5.5 inches, and there's no tag, which is nice. The women's underwear is also on sale.

I prefer the short-sleeve T-shirts, but if you want a long sleeve, this is the T-shirt for you. It's essentially Unbound's short sleeve T-shirt, just long sleeve. All the same descriptions apply here, and many of the same multipack bundles are available. You can grab a 2-pack of long sleeve merino tees for $190 ($40 off).

AI is most powerful when it automates expensive human toil, and few professions rely so heavily on highly trained people doing repetitive work.

Before Sandstone, Sequoia had already partnered with Harvey (AI lawyer), Crosby (AI-enabled law firm), and Ironclad (AI contracting and contract lifecycle management), so weâd seen these dynamics play out firsthand.

Industry observers note that the Sonos Era 100 SL is the exact same speaker as the regular Era 100, minus the microphones and voice control. Ditching those features puts it at a lower cost, especially on sale.

Industry observers note that one of the only home speakers built with spatial audio in mind. The Sonos Era 300 is a great speaker, but transforms when you play Dolby Atmos tracks, activating its upfiring tweeters for more dimensionality.

It has been revealed that sonos' smallest speaker, the Roam 2, is a handheld portable Bluetooth speaker you can basically take anywhere. What separates it from the pack (and Sonos' Bluetooth speakers generally) is that they also connect to Wi-Fi to sync up with your home speakers.

I would argue that the Sonos Move 2 is more of a portable home Bluetooth speaker than a lightweight, compact, throw-it-in-your-bag for a trip to the beach-type speaker like the Roam 2 and Play above. Think of it like a portable, dust and water resistant version of the Era 100.

Sources indicate that the upcoming Sonos Ace Ultra headphones are not on sale, but the capable originals are. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

According to recent reports, this vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

While the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

We are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. New technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

It has been revealed that AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

*We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

The first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

According to recent reports, generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is new.

Sources indicate that A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

It has been revealed that the agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

Industry observers note that it pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

Industry observers note that it cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

It has been revealed that the agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

Sources indicate that it researches those three. One just revealed a new role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

Industry observers note that the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Sources indicate that total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

Sources indicate that this is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

To be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

In a recent development, in last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most important new frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

Two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

According to recent reports, designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

Recent findings suggest that if thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

It has been revealed that soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

Sources indicate that you can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

In a recent development, the AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

According to recent reports, the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. People wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What fresh capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

According to recent reports, how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

Can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

Recent findings suggest that today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

What can you achieve when your aims are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.
